money_at_stake.rationale: The occurrence's own text (Nell's campaign_record) does not carry a dollar figure, so the anchor is the size of the annual revenue base this regulatory campaign binds. The campaign was jointly announced by four national ministries (MIIT, Public Security, Ecology and Environment, SAMR), confirmed by directly re-fetching the CnEVPost launch article this run, which establishes this as a national, industry-wide regulatory action rather than a company- or region-specific one. China's total auto industry revenue for full-year 2025 was RMB 11.1796 trillion (about USD 1.5 to 1.6 trillion at prevailing FX), reported by CPCA Secretary General Cui Dongshu via ChinaEVHome, independently re-fetched this run. That is comfortably GT_100B. CITATION-REPAIR NOTE (2026-08-30): the prior version of this rationale attributed the phrase 'operations and key suppliers' and an 'end of 2026' self-audit reporting deadline to the CnEVPost article. On re-fetch, CnEVPost's text contains neither: no occurrence of 'supplier', 'audit', or any reporting deadline anywhere in the piece. Both assertions are removed and the evidence item that carried them is deleted rather than softened. I deliberately do NOT anchor the band on the automotive testing/inspection/certification (TIC) or homologation market-size estimates that surfaced in search: those ranged from about USD 6.8bn to USD 69bn depending on the paid market-research firm and scope (global TIC vs China-only vs automotive-homologation-only), with no shared methodology and no primary sourcing behind any of them, which is exactly the kind of reasoned-sounding but uncited market-size figure method section 1 and 0.2 warn against. Anchoring instead on the government-reported industry revenue that the mandate now gates is the more conservative, verifiable choice, even though it is a broad denominator rather than a narrow program budget (there is no disclosed compliance budget for this campaign, unlike the icebreaker-program precedent in IMP-20260830-01).

public_reach.rationale: Genuinely mixed, matching the 60 anchor rather than the extremes. For reach: the revenue pool the campaign actually binds (money_at_stake, above) is mostly booked by automakers themselves, and China's largest producers by volume are broadly listed: Great Wall Motor (SSE 601633 / HKEX 2333), BYD (HKEX 1211), and Geely Automobile (HKEX 0175), each independently confirmed against its own stockanalysis.com listing page this run, plus SAIC Motor, NIO, XPeng, Li Auto and the listed European incumbents (Volkswagen, BMW, Mercedes, Stellantis) whose competitive position is the second-order effect Nell's card names, though those additional names were not independently re-verified this run and are not evidenced here. Not scored higher than 60 because a US brokerage account's direct reach into China A-shares specifically (SAIC, BYD's SZSE line) remains a real friction (Stock Connect or QFII access, not a plain buy order), even though the HKEX and ADR lines of the same companies are directly reachable. CITATION-REPAIR NOTE (2026-08-30): the prior version cited a SASAC page (en.sasac.gov.cn/2026/02/05/c_20414.htm) for CATARC's unlisted, central-SASAC-enterprise status as the main 'against reach' consideration. That URL is now unreachable (connection refused on two direct fetch attempts this run) and carries no Wayback Machine snapshot (checked via the archive.org availability API: empty result). The citation does not survive verification and the evidence item is deleted rather than repaired with a substitute source. CATARC's unlisted status is very likely still true (informally corroborated by other outlets found via search this run, none of them opened and cited here) but is deliberately left uncited rather than propped up with a source that was not the one actually verified. The score is HELD at 60 rather than raised on this evidence loss: the A-share access friction above still argues against scoring the reach any higher, even without a citable source for the CATARC-specific mechanism.

capture_odds.rationale: Scored low rather than middling because the empirical backdrop already answers the question this leg asks. China's auto industry average profit margin sank to a historic low of 4.1% in 2025 and dropped further to 2.9% in early 2026, per Caixin Global, directly re-fetched this run, amid what Caixin calls a brutal price war and slowing demand squeezing margins across the sector. A mandatory testing, sample-sealing and proactive-recall regime layered onto an already margin-collapsed, commodity price-war industry is a cost addition applied industry-wide, not a moat for any one listed player: it does not change who wins the price war, and there is no evidence in what I found that it hands pricing power to the automakers who bear it. Not scored at the floor because a real, structural qualification-gating mechanism now exists and could favor already-compliant tier-one suppliers in ways this appraisal has not sized. The entity best positioned to gain from the tighter qualification gate, CATARC, is state-owned and unlisted, though that specific citation did not survive this run's re-verification (see public_reach's citation-repair note) and is not re-asserted here as evidenced. CITATION-REPAIR NOTE (2026-08-30): the prior version of this item also attributed an industry-wide 'RMB 11.2 trillion revenue against RMB 461bn profit' pairing to this same Caixin article. On re-fetch, that aggregate pairing does not appear anywhere in the article; Caixin's own reported figures here are company-specific (BYD: a 19% profit decline to RMB 32.6bn on RMB 804bn revenue), not an industry-wide total. That sentence is removed. The leg's conclusion does not depend on it: the load-bearing fact was always the 4.1%/2.9% margin trend, which is directly quoted and verified.

timing_fit.rationale: Anchored to this occurrence's own anchor_date, 2026-08-27: the campaign is already underway rather than proposed. CnEVPost confirms a one-year campaign was jointly announced by the four ministries; SCMP, the occurrence's own primary source, independently re-fetched this run, confirms the same one-year duration and additionally quotes Vice-Minister Xin Guobin stating that new auto products and technologies would be barred from market entry absent stricter approval procedures, which is itself a concrete, already-in-force compliance mechanism rather than a future deliverable. That places at least one concrete consequence, the market-entry bar, inside the first days of the window, comfortably inside the 2 to 5 year horizon this repo underwrites, and the slower-model-cycle and supplier-requalification consequences Nell's card names as the real thesis would compound over the following one to three years as the new approval regime becomes the operating norm. CITATION-REPAIR NOTE (2026-08-30): the prior version of this leg's evidence asserted that CnEVPost confirmed automakers 'must submit self-audit reports to local authorities by the end of 2026.' On re-fetch, CnEVPost's text contains no such deadline, and a direct re-fetch of the occurrence's own SCMP source (see above) also does not contain it, only that the campaign 'would begin soon' and would run one year. That claim is removed and its evidence item deleted. This appraisal's own notes[] previously stated that CnEVPost corroborated the 'four ministries' framing and 'proactive recall filing'; CnEVPost's only mention of 'recall' is a single reference to a prior, unrelated door-handle recall of 7 million vehicles that predates this campaign, and does not corroborate a proactive-recall-filing requirement under it. That corroboration claim is withdrawn (see notes[] and changelog). Not scored higher than 75 because, absent the deadline-specific detail, the multi-year 'model cycle length changes' thesis remains directionally plausible but is not itself dated or quantified in anything found; only the one-year campaign mechanics, its 2026-08-27 start, and the immediate market-entry-barring statement are concretely dated and sourced.

notes.text: Independent verification of Nell's occurrence claim: fetched CnEVPost (2026-08-27) and the SCMP article Nell cited directly (paywalled excerpt, dated 2026-08-29). Both confirm the core claim, the campaign is real, dated 2026-08-27, and Vice-Minister Xin Guobin is on record saying new auto products/technologies would be barred from market entry absent stricter approval. Two details in Nell's paraphrase, the 'four ministries' framing and 'proactive recall filing,' are corroborated by CnEVPost and by Yahoo/autos.yahoo coverage rather than by the SCMP excerpt itself, which reads as a partial/paywalled fetch. The claim holds; the citation chain for two sub-details runs through corroborating outlets rather than the single named source.

COMPETED is not a dismissal. The money is large (GT_100B, the whole regulated industry revenue base) and reaches listed issuers at a real, if access-constrained, rate (public_reach 60): most volume sits with listed Chinese and international automakers. What keeps this off REACHABLE or PRIME is capture: a record-low 4.1% industry margin and a brutal price war mean a new compliance cost layered on top does not currently look like it sticks as profit anywhere reachable. A chain build here, if one is warranted, should test whether ALREADY-QUALIFIED tier-one suppliers or listed test/certification names (not CATARC, which is unlisted) pick up pricing power from the qualification gate, since that is the one mechanism in the evidence that could move capture_odds rather than just money_at_stake.

RETRACTION, citation-repair pass: the first note above claims the 'four ministries' framing and 'proactive recall filing' are corroborated by CnEVPost. That is false. On a full re-fetch of the CnEVPost article this run, its only occurrence of the word 'recall' describes a PRIOR, unrelated recall of 7 million vehicles for door-handle defects, predating and unconnected to this campaign; the article says nothing about a proactive-recall-filing requirement under the new campaign, and nothing about supplier obligations or a year-end reporting deadline either (zero occurrences of 'supplier' or 'audit' anywhere in the text). This was an unopened-URL failure of exactly the kind method section 1 was amended to catch: the recall and reporting-deadline claims were written from the occurrence card's own paraphrase and then mis-cited to a source that does not say them, rather than verified against the source actually fetched. The two evidence items carrying those claims (money_at_stake and timing_fit, both citing CnEVPost) are deleted, not softened. The occurrence block's own claim (sourced to SCMP by Nell) may still be accurate; this appraisal simply no longer cites CnEVPost as independent corroboration for the supplier, audit and recall-filing specifics, since CnEVPost does not in fact say them.
